Prompt: [WP] In the animal kingdom, Humans are viewed like Witches/Warlocks: they MIGHT help you benevolent in your time of need, or they might eat you alive, or they might save you but keep you forever. So you know just how serious things are when they say to you "Go get a human."
comment:
"Get a human."
Bucky ran faster than ever. He understood the severity of mama's words. Humans were the last resort. Powerful bipedal entities that wielded fire and big sticks. Controlled these elements of the world.
Some are kind. Some are cruel. They might eat you or save you. It was a gamble. A human could save mama. Or skin her alive. But without this gamble, mama would die for sure.
The last Bucky stole a look at mama, she was halfway submerged in the quicksand.
Humans leave traces of themselves everywhere they went. The footprints in the soil. The broken, burnt wood gathered in a pile. The strange structures they erected in clearings. How they could open and close and carry them around was always a mystery to Bucky.
A whiff of human scent reached his nose. Along with all the other signs of human activity. Bucky slowed his movements to a crawl. Creeping ever so carefully towards the human ground. Where the humans, in their strange coverings that could be taken off like a snake sheds its skin, sang songs and clapped.
He bent down in a subservient pose and crawled up to the nearest human. They all turned to him.
This was his moment.
Bucky whined and bowed and placed a paw on a human's lap. Widened his eyes and stared deep into the human's soul within his eyes.
The humans laughed and spoke among themselves. One of them offered him a slice of meat.
Not meat. Help mama. Mama need help. Quicksand. Sinking. Dying.
The human dangled the meat in front of Bucky again.
Not hungry. Save mama. Mama in trouble. Quicksand. Sinking. Dying.
He did his playful soft bite on the human's hand and tried pulling him to where mama was. Thankfully, the human got up and signalled his other humans to follow.
Bucky ran faster than ever. He hoped he wasn't too late. That these humans would come and see mama and pull her out. He got a human like mama asked. Mama better stay alive like he pleaded.
The humans shouted among themselves when Bucky brought them to the quicksand. Mama's head poked just above the surface. Breathing. Mama was breathing. Alive.
Bucky whined.
Mama, I did it! I got humans. I think these humans will help.
A human held out a small black box and aimed it in mama's direction. Click click click. Another broke a branch from a tree and extended it to mama, who bit down on it as the human tugged gently. This human with brown hair tossed a long vine-like thing and coiled it around mama to pull her up.
The men shouted and heaved. Mama was coming up. Bucky could see mama's front paws. Then, with a mighty yank, mama came up.
She was too tired to protest when the humans grabbed them and put both her and Bucky into various poses. The man with the black box stood opposite the rest of them and click click clicked away.
Cheering and slapping each other on the back, the humans made their way back to their clearing.
Bucky sniffed mama to make sure she was okay. When she sniffed him back in return, and both were assured of each other's wellbeing, they headed back to the den.

Prompt: [WP] You were a Necromancer - were, because you forgot to create a contingency for your death. Nobody believes you've actually been slain for good, though, and everybody is running themselves ragged trying to find where you resurrected. Watching from the afterlife, you must admit it's pretty funny.
comment:
Death comes for all, and I was no exception. Even the best necromancers die, eventually. My death was a bit more embarrassing, though. Usually, it takes more than one effort to kill one of us. After all, we specialize in animating the dead, so it stands to reason we would have contingencies for ourselves. Except... I didn't. When I died, I died for real. I had the contingencies on the todo list, but the assassin spoiled everything.
I was in my pajama robes, which were comfortable but not particularly good protection. A man in a black suit and a gritty look in his eye. It was over in a flash, a knife in my eye. I hope the pajamas survived at least. I departed the world that night, but the people who hunt my kind did not know that.
I went through the orientation of my afterlife, and learned I could observe events in the real world. Out of curiosity, I looked at what my killer and his friends were up to, only to find them panicking. A team of magical forensic specialists had descended upon the cave system I lived in. They were intent on finding my backup body or bodies, or a lead on which direction they were. They used the traces of my spirit in my corpse for tracking spells. I saw I don't know how many super high level detect magic spells go off. They found the corpses I was experimenting with, and my god did they give them a lot of attention. They had killed many necromancers, and I guess that they expected me to be far more clever and devious than I actually was.
After watching them spend more money on advanced spell components than I had ever seen in my life, they accepted that I was not hiding in some secret compartment. But their search did not end, rather than reach the true conclusion of my incompetence, they assumed I had access to magic that they did not understand.
Word spread about a necromancer powerful enough to defeat the best diviners in the world. A fever swept the countryside as people scoured the land. There were hilariously many false positives as farmers who knew nothing of magic concluded that they felt my 'presence' in caves. But the organization that killed me responded to each lead with significant effort and attention, revealing little more than bat guano.
I became a legend, a folk villain. Parents told their children that if they did not behave, I would take them away and use their bodies as puppets. My legend grew so significant that people searching for me actually turned up a few genuine necromancers. But still, I eluded them. The cagey genius who might still one day unmake the world, if given a chance.
I wondered if they would ever accept the truth. After years of hunting me, I think they were all too committed to the idea of me as a super necromancer to ever question the assertion. If only they could appreciate how many tears they caused me to shed in laughter.

Prompt: [WP] The prophecy foretold that The Great Evil would awaken 1000 years after his original defeat. As it turns out, the people took this very seriously, so when he awakened, he was met with an army of blessed knights, an evil containment system, and two dozen automated holy turrets aimed at him.
comment:
One thousand years ago, the holy knight Gareth of Deepwood, wielder of the Chrysanthemum Blade, leader of the Circle of the Sacred Sky, and the fated Seventh Son of the Seventh Son, laid the demon lord Roshanet low. As the blade was plunged deep into the fiend's chest, he issued forth Prophecy.
"Know you this, Children of Men, there is no blade of mortal make that can truly slay the True Lord of Demons. A thousand years from now, when you are dust and none remember even your names, I shall return and deliver ruination unto all!"
Naturally, there were those who felt that this was naught but bluster - an attempt to claw back a victory from what was truthfully a sound defeat and assuage a badly wounded demonic pride. These people were summarily drummed out of the rulership of the kingdom, stripped of noble titles and lands, and their possessions forfeited to fund the Chrysanthemum Institute. The finest arcanists, priests, and warriors came together under this banner, with the sole stated goal of ensuring that Roshanet's little threat came to nothing.
First and foremost, Gareth's sword was willingly given up to the institute for study. The arcanists spent decades studying the various spells woven into the blade, figuring out what was the exact magic that made it so effective against demons. Each enchantment and blessing was applied to separate bamboo rods by the priests, which were then issued to the warriors. Lesser fiends were summoned on an industrial scale for scientific testing. Each time a rod was found to be effective, the spell would be noted and applied in combination with others to create effective mass-production demon-slaying weapons.
Next, there was the Chronicler corp. Their job was keeping accurate track of the precise date and time of Roshanet's defeat, and using that to extrapolate the rough date and time he would return. In the event that the Chrysanthemum Institute, its home country, or both fell before that time, they also were tasked with ensuring that future generations would be prepared to deal with the demon lord. Additionally, a subset was tasked with studying other powerful demons, the effect they had on the world around them, and the signs that could be used to predict their movements.
Finally, there was the warrior training. Gareth himself headed this group at the beginning, training soldiers to combine swordsmanship with spellcraft, though he knew that most would not be blessed with his natural arcane might. He worked with the kingdom's most skilled artificers to build support units that the soldiers would be able to use to supplement their weaknesses. Some decided to forego balancing their loadouts to better specialize - arcane snipers, juggernauts, barrier masters and engineers. Eighty years after the Institute opened its doors, Gareth passed away surrounded by friends, family, those he inspired, and most importantly those who would carry on his purpose.
Nine-hundred-ninety-nine years after Roshanet fell before Gareth's band of heroes, the Signs and Portents were read by the Chroniclers. One year and one day hence, the Demon Lord would rise again. The exact location where the demon lord would re-emerge was determined, and the Guardians got to work. Engineers began the process of constructing turrets, barrier masters carved arcane sigils around the spot spiraling out for miles, with weaker sigils built in depth. Prompt: [WP] While other god's shrines are magnificent, yours is a bit too humbling. And yet a little girl visits you every year after stumbling upon it, never missing a year even as she grows old. Deeply moved, you decide to give her a parting gift greater than what any other God would dare to give.
comment:
It wasn’t much of a shrine, really. More like a mistake someone forgot to clean up—a toppled stone, a clump of moss, a flower that bloomed too early and just stayed. The others had gold. Marble. Columns so tall they made you feel small before you even got inside, which was probably the point. Me? I had… well, dirt. Dirt and one loyal visitor.
She was small when she first stumbled in, hair wild and clothes half-tucked like she’d wrestled a tornado and lost. She looked at the stone—my stone—and said, "Huh. That’s weird." Then she sat down, right there in the mud, and started talking.
Talking! To me! The god of—well, that’s complicated. Not something grand like thunder or love or, I don’t know, cheese. (Cheese is big. People love cheese.) No, I was the god of Small Forgotten Things. Buttons in gutters. The last sip of tea. Shrines no one visits.
Except her.
Every year, she came back. Not with gold or incense or whatever the fancy gods demanded. Just her. Sitting. Talking. Telling me about school, her parents fighting, how her brother put a frog in her shoe, how she put the frog in his bed, how she didn’t even feel bad about it. (I liked that one. Feisty.) She didn’t ask for anything. Never prayed. Never begged. Just talked, like we were old friends. And I—I listened.
Years passed. She grew up. The wild hair got tamer, the clothes more put-together. But she always came back. Always sat in the mud, even when she was wearing something too nice for mud. "You’re the only one who gets it," she said once, leaning back against my stone. "You don’t try to fix me. You just… listen."
And oh, did I listen. To everything. Her first love (some guy named Marco—didn’t like him, too smug), her first heartbreak (Marco again, predictable), her first job (terrible boss, good coffee). I listened as her visits grew longer apart, but she always came back. Always.
Then, one day, she showed up different. Older. Frailer. A cane tapping against the stone as she lowered herself down. She sat there, breathing heavy, and said, "Well, old friend. This might be it."
It? I felt the panic before I could stop it. Gods aren’t supposed to panic. We’re supposed to be all-knowing, all-powerful. But all I knew was that my only believer was leaving, and I was powerless to stop it.
"I wish I could stay longer," she said, smiling at the stone. "But I’m tired. And you—you’ve been enough. More than enough."
No. No, no, no. Not enough. Never enough. Not for her. Not for my only visitor, my only friend.
So I did the one thing gods aren’t supposed to do. I meddled.
She closed her eyes, leaning against the stone, and when she opened them again—well. She wasn’t old anymore. Or frail. Or tired. She looked down at her hands, smooth and strong, and then at me—really at me, for the first time.
"You—" she started, but I didn’t let her finish.
"Go," I said, the words rumbling through the stone. "Live. Love. Be. And don’t forget me."
She laughed. Loud, full, free. "Forget you? Never."
And then she ran, young again, back into the world. My little shrine, my small forgotten place, felt quiet. But not empty.
Never empty.

Prompt: [WP] A human accidentally wanders into a Fae realm. The fae in responce give him disgusting food, ugly clothing, an uncomfortable bed, etc. The human has never been treated better and thinks the Fae are being nice
comment:
Ben worked over the bowl of slop with great enthusiasm. His spoon practically a blur as he took down mouthful after mouthful with nothing but a smile on his face. The being that stood over his shoulder could only wince as they watched the human consume the gruel. They simply could not understand how this human could seem to enjoy it so. It was the scraps of the last great feast- bone meal from the roasted boar, ground bits of brown bread, all of it soaked in the greasy, salty dredges of the gravy boat. The meal was barely fit for a starved hunting hound, but this human seemed to enjoy every spoonful of it.
"Excuse me," They said as they covered their mouth to keep themselves from gagging. "I have to speak to someone. I shall return, son of none."
A thumbs up was given from Ben, who had a mouthful of the slop, but did not look their way as they departed from the room.
"Well, Tiberius?" Another strange figure said as soon as they stepped out of the room. Their skin like bark and clothes flowing like rushing water. "Is the human disgusted yet?"
"No," Tiberius said, trying to keep their own breakfast down as they walked away from the room with their companion. The leaves they wore clinging tightly to an elongated form. "The mortal consumes the scraps as if its a grand feast itself. I am at a loss, Verin."
Verin's hand came to their forehead, rubbing at it. "You cannot be serious. The human is eating it all?"
"He might ask for seconds."
Verin winced. "Do we have to feed him dirt to get him to be displeased with us? Is he even human?"
"You know the laws of hospitality bind us from giving him anything but what may grace our own tables," Tiberius said. "I thought the coarse undergarments would drive him away. He said he was just glad to have underwear that didn't have holes in them."
"I'll have several stones added to his bed," Verin said.
"Don't bother," Tiberius said with a dismissive hand wave. "He seems content to sleep on rugs by the fireplace in his room."
"This is absurd," Verin said. "We must banish this mortal from our realm at once. Damn the rules of hospitality."
"The price to pay for that is too steep," Tiberius said as they glanced back at the room where Benjamin sat, eating his meal. "What kind of life has this man led?"
Benjamin watched the strange not-men from the corner of his eye, as he shovelled the food into his mouth. He wasn't stupid, he knew he was getting the worst that they could get away with giving him. No one would waste their best on someone like him after all.
But they were underestimating how much better their worst was compared to what he was used to. This food was terrible, by their standards, but it was plentiful and nutritious and there was no one slapping the bowl from his hands if he took too long to eat it. The clothes were rough in comparison to theirs, but they were whole and he hadn't had to fight others to get them from the back of a dead man. And while the bed was his and his alone so also was the entire room in which it sat, and though the bed was just too soft for comfort, the rugs in front of the fire felt just right.
Benjamin's spoon scraped the bottom of the bowl, unnoticed by the two not-men who continued to debate how to make him uncomfortable enough to leave. They didn't know, he could tell, just what existence he had led up until his flight into this place, however accidental it was. He ran his fingers over the cold iron that encircled his wrist, that these strangers had recoiled from even the slightest touch of.
They didn't know that to Benjamin, this place might as well be the Heaven that the preachers said a slave like him would never reach.

Prompt: [WP] When a mining colony was established on a barren, uninhabitable planet, the humans threatened war if it was not abandoned immediately. Apparently this planet, which they call "Earth", is sacred to them.

Our scans had indicated that Planet 410-E-N had been previously inhabited by intelligent life, but had not been so for many centuries due to high levels of harmful radiation. Thus, in accordance with Galactic Federation law, we publicly submitted a formal mining claim for the barren planet's surprisingly vast amount of underground resources. After waiting the required period of contest, and after receiving no protest of this claim, we sent a small number of colonization ships to begin extracting resources. Nothing about this colonization had been any different from the countless other missions that we, or anyone else in the Federation, had conducted since the third galactic unification event. Such was the first few seasons on 410-E-N as the colony flourished on the planet's surface, trading outposts were established in low planetary orbit, and our hope for revitalizing our economy grew just a little more.
We were unaware of the planet's cultural significance to what was a previously unknown species we now all know as "humans" or "Terrans". As I'm sure you're aware, this species was previously known as, "ape-kin", but is no longer due to the most recent Federation hate-speech guidelines... sorry, I digress... Anyways, almost a local year after the colony's founding, we had our first contact with the humans when a Terran Republic patrol warped into the system without detection via a previously unnoticed FTL beacon located by 410-E-N's moon. Their sudden appearance caused a near collision with a Umar Kingdom freighter, which fired warning shots at them as they assumed they were under attack from pirates. This unfortunately also marked our first conflict with the Terran Republic, resulting in the Umar ship being heavily damaged along with 16 system police vessels that responded to the distress calls.
It was only when a Federation war strike group warped in many moments later in which the Terran ship ceased it's firing and made hailing attempts. Apparently, from what we were initially able to understand via our auto-translators, 410-E-N was a highly sacred religious site for the Terrans. "Earth", as they called it, was their birth-planet, and although it was unoccupied, they considered it as a core planet for their species. It was still inhabitable to them due to their lower radiation resistance, but they apparently made annual "pilgrimages" to the planet to reflect on their roots and pay tribute to those who were unable to flee when some sort of large nuclear disaster claimed the lives of most the living creatures on the planet.
After an entire daylight cycle on 410-E-N, negotiations with the Terrans still had not made much progress. Their language was so different from the 26 planet-states of the Federation that most of the day had been spent waiting for the translators to interpret their speech and for clarifying questions to be sent back and fourth. One point of speech had been made extremely clear however, and that was the Terran's demand for us to complete vacate the planet and return it to it's pre-colonized state immediately. Resistance to this demand would be considered an act of war.
The Federation still did not have much of a first-contact protocol back then, as you may remember that prior to the humans's appearance, it was widely taught that life only existed within our small star cluster, and so we already had made contact with each other before the Federation was even a thing. We had seen their patrol of 6 relatively medium-sized starships defeat the Umar and system police ships with ease, and so we obviously had the brains to not immediately begin attacking them after their threat. We had no idea of their ships's capabilities, and level of technology. The star admiral of the strike group was eventually able to ease tensions and arrange a proper cease-fire and ceasing of mining activities until a diplomatic team could arrive on the scene.
When they did arrive after many tense and uncomfortable moments, the Terrans had seemed to calm down as the translators indicated a more "polite and inviting" tone shift from the previous "threatening and aggressive" reading. Our diplomats began with gaining more general knowledge about them as a species with the underlying goal of figuring out their technological abilities, how much of a threat they were to the Federation, and if they could be persuaded to let us keep 410-E-N. We learned that they were fairly close to our technological level, except with an emphasis of using more ballistic-type weapons and nuclear-steam engines for their energy creation. We were a bit disturbed to learn that they were able to easily take down our ships simply because their culture was extremely militarized. They apparently suffered from the irritations of piracy as much as we did, and so thought the Umar and system police were some pirates with "odd technology".
410-E-N was indeed their birth planet, and they had evacuated it about 300 local years ago after an extremely large nuclear power plant in the antarctic region of the once-green planet suffered a catastrophic meltdown. This caused the entire mostly-icy continent to begin melting, raising the planet's sea levels and contaminating the ocean water with extremely radioactive run off. Though the destruction of the planet was not immediate, the humans simply did not have enough time to relocate their population elsewhere. Their star-travel abilities were relatively lacking and was restricted to non-FTL speeds back then. Their closest habitable star system was 4.2 light years away and with their primary energy source now poisoning them, they only had enough resources and time to evacuate about 10% of their population. The remainder had died on Earth from either the radiation sickness or worldwide flooding.
It took a few more local daylight cycles to come to agreements, but eventually an extremely long list of terms and conditions was laid out by the Terran Republic, which was wearily accepted by the Federation. The highlight consisted of us still having mining rights over the system, but only on a smaller, red planet in the system designated as 410-E-O. We could also have mining rights a smaller ninth planet in the system, as the Terrans did not consider it as a planet for unknown reasons. As scans showed that the two planets had a considerable amount of precious elements much deeper into their crusts, it was a concession we could accept.
Additionally, we learned that although the Terrans had successfully colonized in their neighboring system in what they called, "Proxima Centauri B", a sloppy name at that, their colonization efforts were not going well in recent years. A team of our experimenters had actually found that they would've only been able to sustain themselves for another century or so before collapse due to a variety of failures. Thus, they requested probationary statehood into the Federation, with a small amount of subsidies in the forms of loans to help them improve and maintain their colony. Though we were initially not as willing to allow them this privilege, their additional offer to greatly contribute to anti-piracy patrols was one we could not pass up, as none of us were anywhere as adept as they were with military tactics and tradition. This is why they make up 70% of our current security forces although only consisting around 16% of Federation citizenry. Because of them, piracy is at the lowest point in any time in history and so is general unrest galaxy-wide.
So, with that brief history in mind, we now come to the topic at hand: Their probationary status is up for review in the next coming days, so we must now consider whether we should cancel it, extend it, or promote them to full statehood. Though our first contact was rough, I do believe they've earned their place. However, Federation law does require that full states have the privilege of using our health and well-being budget to ensure the habitability of their core worlds. This does mean that we will be obligated to restore 410-E-N to a full state of habitability, which may cost us hundreds of trillions of credits just to clear the radiation spills and reintroduce local fauna, which the Terrans at least already have samples of.
Are we willing to promote them for their hard work at the cost of our entire health and well-being budget for the next 1.4 Federation cycles? What say the council?

Being away smog, traffic, garbage smells and everything in-between cleared my senses more than they ever had. With our toxic living conditions, no wonder people who embrace the natural wonder of the world would recoil at fruits of our own doom. This toy wasn't just a dumb ball I rolled around when I was five, it was a symbol, and the message of a people who would destroy their own home for a scrap of entertainment.

"This is..."
I muttered to myself, peering closer to my client. Her strings of fate lay bare for me to see, my magic caressing each one with care. Wound within was the obvious mark of a curse, black threads choking and warping her strings.
But that wasn't what had given me pause. The string they mainly tied to was that of life. The one that guided how long a person would live for naturally, before their body finally gave out. It had been changed to make her appear vastly older, a wizened crone instead of the young lady she was.
This curse had infected it deep. Turning it, and twisting ever so slightly revealed the core within, turned the same black as this curse itself. I shuddered at the implications. Who could use such power that it could corrupt the very laws of the universe itself? I didn't know, and I didn't want to know. They could have done so much worse to this lady. This aging was almost a kindness in comparison.
Still, she had hired me to fix it. A costly service, but I was good at what I did. I had a perfect success rate so far, and this would be no different.
Shaking my head, I went to work. Ingredients flew off the shelves to me, mixing in a floating bowl. I added sparks of my own magic, letting the basis of my work take hold. With a final stir, light orange mist poured out, surrounding us.
It touched the curse, its taut lines loosening. Not enough to pull it off, but I didn't need that. It was enough to move the line powering it. Instead of it feeding from ambient mana, I linked it to itself. The loop would make it devour the very magic keeping it together.
Within seconds, the effect was apparent. Her skin tightened, wrinkles fading away. Thinning hair became full, sweeping away its greyed locks to show her natural red locks. Her rigid posture relaxed, a smile gracing her now youthful face.
I kept an eye on it, especially how it had corrupted a core of a string of fate. But to my shock, it didn't just disappear. The entire core crumpled, the string changing shape. To my disbelieving eyes, it didn't tail off as it was supposed to. It bent down, forming a loop. The string of fate didn't end.
-----
I threw myself into my research upon seeing that. I sought to find any evidence this had happened before. What could it mean? There had to be a reason for this. I hadn't let the lady know what had happened, as I just couldn't understand it. How could I tell her a string had changed, without knowing exactly what it meant?
Yet no matter how hard I looked, I couldn't work out what had happened. There was nothing. Not even a hint of a legend. This had happened, and now I had to deal with it.
Without knowing what had happened, I had to experiment. And experiment I did, using myself as a test subject as always. I had enough notes to recreate the curse, and set it on myself. I twisted open my own strings, to watch it happen.
But it didn't infect it, as I expected. The curse simply warped it. It barely touched my core, unable to truly infect it. My core just turned black, the same colour as the curse. The same colour as all curses.
And that is when it hit me. I had seen similar before. A rare case, someone affected by two curses. One had been subtle, lingering for years. And the only way I had seen it was when the other had interacted with it, and revealed its existence.
This was the same. The exact same interaction between curses. They had linked, because they were both affecting lifespan. But one was physical, the other deeply rooted. So deeply rooted, it was seen as natural.
I broke my own curse, watching the string undergo the same change as the lady's had. I meditated on it, sending my consciousness through what it would mean, drifting through the various futures.
And in all, I saw the same fundamental thing. My age became static. I was forever young, my body constantly rejuvenating.
Aging wasn't a natural law. It was a curse. A curse far older and greater than anything that seemed possible. And I had worked out how to remove it.
This was dangerous knowledge to have. The secret of immortality was mine, and mine alone to know. The question now was, what was the right thing to do with this knowledge?

I noticed out of the corner of my eye the way the barber changed the grip on the razor. "Gentlemen. This man has already paid for his shave. Soap, lather, aftershave. Your business with him will have to wait until. I. Am. Done."
I smiled at myself in the mirror, as a droplet fell from the razor. Behind me was the old barber, Jonah Dalton, standing straight, arms bent upwards, as if to say, "Are we clear?" He stared at the mirror reflecting the barbershop behind us.
In the middle of the parlor stood three men in baggy jackets and caps pulled down low, hands in their pockets, fidgeting. For a moment, no one made a move or uttered a word. Then, as if God had clicked play, their eyes glinted, and their bodies seemed to untense.
"Alright, Mr. Dalton, we got you," said the one in the middle. As he took his hands out of his pockets and turned, the others joined him in sitting on the stools off to the side, their jackets swishing against each other. "But right after you’re done, we need to talk to that kid about some hitters."
"That's none of my business," said Jonah, grinning, gesticulating, slicing at the air beside him. As he smiled, the dark brown skin at the sides of his face crinkled into familiar folds, his eyes appearing beady yet somehow sharp through his thick-lensed spectacles.
"Now, let me get back to business," he says, and returns his focus to my shave. He drags the razor across my cheek, that familiar grainy scratch shouting out in the quiet shop. As the sound filled the air around us, he mumbled without looking away from my head.
"They sent three just to talk to you."
"Yeah, I see that," I mutter.
"Those boys always come in here hunting for rookies, you know," he said.
"Oh, I know, Mr. Dalton," I say, "But I've got a surprise for them."
"Tens only, I hope," the old barber says, "I don't want to see any cut corners or messes. Especially their faces."
"I never touch their faces," I say, "You know that, Mr. Dalton."
"They'll get you with the fingerprints, you know."
"I know, Mr. Dalton."
The three men shift uncomfortably behind us, their identical fitted caps stating flatly, "We're New Yorkers. That's all you need to know."
In one brisk motion, Mr. Dalton whisked my apron off. He swept at my nape and said, "Good luck on your business, boy. Hope you've got a few Judges in your pocket."
"'Course I do, sir," I say, smiling and getting up.
As I head out with the three men, they're excitedly talking amongst themselves.
"Yo, Mr. Dalton just said it, though."
One of them tapped me on the arm, "Ey, you got Judges?"
"I got three Judge rookie Topps, and even a rookie Jeter."
The barbershop door jingles behind us as the three start hollering with joy.

Prompt: [WP] Everyone thinks that Runes and Glyphs are a "poor man's magic". You are an average guy that enjoys writing computer programs that got isekai'd to this world, and you quickly realize that runes are tools to modify the source code of reality.
comment:
It's not a keyboard and monitor anymore, but a quill with an inkwell and a scroll. I still find ways to scream at it.
Dropping my head down into my desk I sigh and recite the words of my prof. "Icheton works with Jeriton while Oratition is best with Hexamogon not Lafiet." Looking at my 'script' I mixed up Hexamogon with Garla, again.
This wasn't like computers where I could backspace though and type it out properly. I had to start from scratch. Again.
Sighing I roll my head to the side and look at my friend Agememenon. "I hate this stuff."
He shakes his head and goes. "I don't understand why you don't just use the proper rune combinations that have already been determined. Magic doesn't have to be this hard."
How do I explain computers to a person from a society that would drop their jaw in shock at ball bearings. "Old habits I guess." Looking up at my 'rubber' ducky I carved from wood and silently pleaded with him to help me along.
"Your totem isn't working that great. Perhaps if you enchant it like I told you too it would be a better sounding board."
Lifting my head up I shook my head. "That's not how it works." Going back to writing out the runes in sequence and hoping against hope that inspiration would strike me blind between the eyes.
It wouldn't be the first time it had happened.
My innovation of creating a self filling quill came from a drunken tyraid into the glyph system that they'd been using for irrigation. Even now everyone used my patented refillable quill, gaining me substantial profit. Although for a simple reason I was using an ordinary channelled quill.
Now however I was endeavouring towards something even more revolutionary, if I could only get it...ah ha! The runes weren't working because of the central controlling rune! If I inverted it then. "Eureka!" Standing up in joy.
My friend looked over excitedly. He'd heard me use that word before. "What is it? What have you done?"
Smiling at him as I touched the scrolls runes and moved my quill backwards across them. His eyes went wide. "This will change everything." He looked up at me. "Again."
Yes I'd created something truly revolutionary in this medieval time of need. We both watched as the ink on the scroll went back into my quill filling up the channel within.
Despite all of my grueling hours of work it was worth it. I'd created a backspace rune combination.
After I created the backspace rune combination I became even more famous than before. All of that was rather tiring if I was honest. The money was nice I'll admit, afforded me to live in a lap of luxury not available to common folk.
I now gathered the interest of professors who'd scoffed at my ideas and machinations. Calling me fool. Or marginally talented, to sooth their aching egos. Now with the ability to 'save ink time' and 'retract words' as they were calling it. My method of scripting was becoming quite popular.
Just means I had more competition really.
Not much competition mind you, they were still medieval magical scholars contending with an Information Age former programmer. So when I created an interface to 'write' a script on a scroll, using a very crude looking typewriter. Well. Shit just got out of hand.
Combining that with my backspace rune combo and ink refilling spell, I revolutionized the written word. Not only could mages create one off spells you didn't have to memorize. I showed a merchant how to craft one for ordinary folk. Which a commission on each one sold of course.
Books became wide spread. Literacy rates shot up like fireworks. People became more educated and knowledgeable. Now literature was available to the common man like never before and schools teaching words and languages sprung up like daisies over the intervening years.
With my typewriter I began scripting, no that's not right anymore, I began typing out spell combinations others hadn't dreamed of. I was becoming known as The Book Mage. The The was very important as others were using books to be mages after my invention, I was creating those books and spells.
I soon opened my own research building where we dabbled in all sorts of things. From potions to floating glyphs, runes made to slide things along a piece of clothe like a conveyor belt.
Within ten years of my magically typing typewriter we transformed this little backwater kingdom into The place of magical knowledge and research. Scholars from all over flocked to our innovative seaside kingdom. We became known as a mage city in no time. Where one out of ten of the residents were magically gifted.
I sat on my balcony looking out over the garden district. My typewriter sitting comfortably on the table. A simple script I'd been working on for the past five years finally coming together.
Sipping my tea I smiled at myself. "A third rate programmer." I chuckled at my old profs words in my last life. I had a life of wealth privilege and respect. A home with servants and a footman. My magical inventions dotted the region and I assumed the world.
Turning back to my typewriter, now christened an arcane scripter, and typed in the last few runes. I've created a new language recently. More compact so it could fit on a stamp, or a printing press. This typewriter was one of five we'd created to write the language. It wasn't really like a normal one at all. More circular in its printing style. Typing in the last few modern runes I crossed my fingers and pulled the small gem encrusted lever. The typewriter hummed and jiggled.
The scroll next to it caught the magical explosion that knocked me off of my chair.
Coughing and waving away the purple smoke I sighed as I stood up and then looked in surprise. "It worked?" Looking down at the page beside the arcane scripter, attached with a piece of cloth I'd designed for this purpose. There sat the symbol I'd created. Perfectly mimicking the one now burnt in the machine. "Eureka!"
Agememenon stood at the door looking down at the ruined arcane scripter, then up at me. "Oh no. I know what that word brings." He stated with a smile.
Grinning like a mad man. "Innovation." I'd created a copy and paste spell.
Never in my Isekai'd life did I ever imagine I'd be this kind of mage at forty.
A stamp mage. No seriously. I've got stamps that'll cause wind storms, cause hail if I use the proper combination. Even a fire tornado. Cause. Why not? You gotta enjoy what you do when it comes to life. Right?
Stamps had exploded into life after combination rune magic came around. Oh we still used glyphs too. Those were just used like some kinda weird graffiti magic. Lay down a stencil, paint it in with a huge mop like a giant Calligrapher. Then you've created a focus or a combination of them to rearrange a city block in some weird way to make staircases infinite. Glyphs were mainly used in war. They'd gone from moderately powerful spells only advanced mages could use. To being stamped on rubble to turn them into bombs that rivalled ICBM's. Some were outright banned.
Some mages managed to create staffs that were stamps. Or ones with multiple stamps. Wands were all but gone. The spoke spell was becoming so intricate thanks to the assignment of words to runic combinations, magic had morphed once more.
Now though, thanks to my copy paste spell. Manufacturing death books had come into play.
I'd gone from doe eyed innocent researcher into accidental arms developer. I'll admit though. I never let my copy paste spell get out of hand. It did that all on its own.
Now every hedge mage, or two bit conjurer who could muster enough power was drafted into the war against our neighbour. The reason for said war? Well. Me.
Not specifically me, but my innovations, my way of thinking. New vs old in a way that made far off mages jealous and angry. They told their leiges which made them angry. Now thanks to short tempers and expansionist policies, or warring cultures. They wanted what we had.
The city of Gestalt was the most powerful city in the known world. Our king had since allied our small nation with the local emperor of a much bigger one for protection and it was his lands they were pounding.
Thankfully they saw me as too valuable to lose. So I was still in my little research academy turning out mass produced bombs in the form of runic sheets of paper. War as it turns out, turned a profit.
With those profits I became altruistic. Using magical runic and glyph combinations made of wood for long lasting spells. Things like umbrellas that flared to life after the user spun the gem. Irrigation canals that ran on aqueducts and timers to water the crops. Pressure systems. Ways of forging copper and steel at a rate that simply boggled the medieval mind.
Magic wasn't the only game in town either. Since the literacy rate shot up, inventions sprung up left right and center. Mundane people made things that ran off water, steam even! I had no part in those. Most people other than me came up with amazing inventions and innovations.
Gestalt was a city nestled in a bay. Capital of a small kingdom in the bosom of an empire. We had everything and wanted for nothing. With the war going in our favour we may even conquer the world, by proxy.
I couldn't care less though about conquering.
I had one thing more magical than anything I'd created. I had my wife. My three daughters, one a budding mage. Two incredibly smart. One wanting to be a knight. The other a painter. My wife of ten years is a well-known poet and a business woman herself.
We lived in luxury, not opulence. I had seen the lengths of disconnection that did to others of my time.
My money went to funding schools, public works and of course the tax that went to the kingdom. No business man gets away from that in this time.
Money never interested me too much anyway.
I was happiest tinkering in my personnel workshop. The Refilling Quill® at my side. A book to write in and a cup of tea as I looked out over the garden district.

She punched the air so hard she was briefly off the ground. "YES!" She put her notebook down and the napkin fell.
Rebecca was grinning like a maniac. No longer could anyone keep her from her reading.
A few years of normal time later, Rebecca had practically become a supernatural being herself. But we'll save that for another... well, time.

Prompt: [WP] You've been "trapped" in a "VR" game for years, learnt magic, had a family, etc. But now they've "rescued" you from it all. Waking up on the hospital bed you reflexively cast a shield. Which works.
comment:
Okay, that works, which is bad.
I try several other magic, and they all work.
I cast telepathy, and read the minds of the people going in and out of my room.
Nobody knows a thing.
They all think that I have been trapped in a VR game, when the helmet malfunctioned, and fried a part of my brain.
It is a miracle in their eyes, that I woke up.
But I know the reality of things...
My soul has been yanked out of my body, and I lived a looong life in another world.
I had a life, a family, everything was good there, and I want back.
"Son!" my mother cries on my chest.
I can finally sit up, my muscles starting to regain some strength.
My mother...mom, has been working hard these 3 years, yes only 3 years passed in this world, to keep me alive.
Many wanted to shut off the life support after a year, but not her.
She knew I will be back.
Maybe magic while not apparent, really exists here, and these "motherly intuition" and "6th sense" stuff, are actually dream magic, or divination?
I can hear her thoughts, I can feel her happiness.
How do I tell her I lived tens of thousands of years, and have a family that could build an entire country in our world...and that my feelings for this life are...almost non-existent?
"I know you have lived a life in the game, but you will have to come to terms that this is your real life." the therapist starts. It's been 6 months since I came back, and I can walk, and eat and talk on my own, but they can see it.
How unaffected I am by everything here. And the fact that I spend all my time researching the game company doesn't help with the impressions.
"I can understand that, but please, if I felt, saw, experienced an entire life there... Why would that be any less real, than what is here?" I ask her.
She falls silent. Yeah, this always happen.
But I don't care, I will go back, no matter what.
It's been a year, and basically I confirmed that magic exists on Earth, its just dormant, and much more difficult to communicate with.
But it exists, and it is almost stronger, and purer that what we had on Eldria.
I can do it. I can open a portal back home.
"Honey! I am home!" mom says from downstairs.
She spent each free moment of hers with me...
Ever since dad died when I was a kid...we were there for each other, the two of us against the world.
"What are you doing?" she asks, coming into my room, watching me scribble the runes.
"Come, mom. I will show you your great-great-great-great-grandkids, and your daughter-in-law." I saw.
She frowns, then smile, willing to humor me, before gasping...as a portal opens.
"Let's go...home." I say.
She follows without a moment of hesitation...
Maybe this is why I have been returned...to get mom to a better place.

Prompt: [WP] "I... am the last of my kind. Our planet, our home, destroyed by war, a testament to-" "What? No you aren't." "...Pardon?" "Dude, your people have like 2, 3 colony planets the next system over."
comment:
A dark cloud encircled the globe, beneath it the red shined through here and there. Signs of volcanoes spewing unimaginable amounts of lava.
Kaltis watched his world die through the porthole of the spacecraft. He wanted to peel his eyes from the window and look at the creature that had abducted him, be he couldn't.
"I... am the last of my kind. Our planet, our home, destroyed by war, a testament to-" he was going to say hate, but the alien spoke.
"What? No, you aren't." The aliens voice came through the little pin on its collar.
Kaltis tore his gaze from the window and observed the genderless two armed quadruped. The operator of the ship was still in its chair wearing those goggles not moving.
"...Pardon?" Kaltis wondered if there were other survivors on the ship. The creature had said that it'd only taken Kaltis. Had it been lying?
"Dude, your people have like two, three colony planets the next system over."
"How can this be? We never traveled the stars." Kaltis walked to his host and stood beside it.
"Oh, your people were one many colonies. Your people’s home world is doing just fine. That’s where I'm taking you." The pin spoke and the creature sat perfectly still.
The light brown fur covering its body looked soft. The nose on the end of its short snout looked wet and it's toothless mouth hung slightly open.
It was a lot to take in. In a way, it made perfect sense.
They had been able to find evidence of evolution for every creature on their planet but themselves. That was why the religion of Taotilen had been so pervasive, there was no proof that they hadn't been put on their planet by the Goddess Taot.
Kaltis thought of his failed negotiations and how the price of his failure had been the deaths of billions. He couldn't imagine a world where those zealots hadn't ruined everything. He'd spent his life a rebel and now... would he get a chance to live among his people again without the yoke of the Taotilen?
"Why do they want me?" Kaltis asked. Were they going to punish him for his failure? Were they going to save him for his efforts?
"It's a government museum that sponsored this grab. They wanted someone from the colony that could speak on your people’s development. A very standard check in." The pin chirped.
"Did they know?" He asked the alien.
"Did they know that you all were about to kill yourselves? Nah man. No way. They might have stepped in. They had no idea, I'd have stepped in to try something but there was nothing in the playbook to deal with what was going on. I gave you as much time as I could before I grabbed you," for the first time the creature moved, it's hands raised the goggles and it looked up at Kal with it's metallic chrome eyes and its mouth closed tight while the pin said, "For what it’s worth, I thought you were gonna pull it off. I'm sorry that it didn't work out."
Kaltis nodded, thought about touching its shoulder but didn't. He walked over the window and looked down at his world in its death throes.
"I chose you of all I observed, you had nobody too close. You have a good heart. Billions deserved another chance, but I could only choose one. I am sorry." Kaltis startled at the feeling of its four fingered hand on his shoulder.
"How long will we travel?" He still could not look away from the dark sphere below.
"For you, it will feel like a nap."
Kal felt a coolness in his bones and his vision faded.

Prompt: [WP] An orphan develops the habit of talking to the moon as if it were a parent. Just telling it about their day, and occasionally announcing milestones in their life, like their admission to college and the like. Unbeknownst to them, the moon has been listening all along, and it's so very proud.
comment:
The first time the Moon heard a voice, it was Oliver, when he was a small seven-year-old kid. All alone in the crumbling orphanage's creaky attic, curled up by the dusty window. Gazing at the Moon.
"Hey, mom? Dad? Is anyone up there? I just wanna say I got first prize for my school's art contest. Are you proud?"
The Moon listened. And she was proud. Alas, she could not hug him. Acknowledge his words. For she was the Moon in the sky, far away from the Earth. So, she did the only thing she could do.
Shine the reflected light of the Sun into the window. At him. A gentle moonglow that bathed a small circle where Oliver sat.
Unaware, he nodded off. Only to be discovered in the dead of the night by a matron who scooped him off to bed. A matron who never once looked up to the sky to see the Moon shining where Oliver once slept in the attic.
The boy would come again the next night. He told the Moon about the bullies at school, the books he loved, the way the rain smelled on the pavement. Some nights, he cried, his voice small and broken.
The moon ached to answer, to reach down with beams of silver light and cradle the boy in its glow. To provide comfort. The embrace of a proud parent. But she could only shine through the window of the attic, as she had always done when he spoke to her. All she could give to the one person who talked to her regularly, whose voice had somehow reached her when the billions of humans on the earth did not, was a small shine.
Through his visits in the attic, the Moon watched him grow. To a gangly teenager who held up a crumpled cert proudly, telling her that he won his high school's science fair. Of the curious contraption he built with scraps and broken pieces, mainly discarded by classmates who were well-off. Classmates who wore brand new clothes, emblazoned with fancy names he didn't know. He had beaten all odds, beaten the expensive, shiny machines that rich, snobby bully at school had paid others to do.
The Moon swelled with pride. Glowing a little brighter, bathing him in a soft light. The closest thing to a silent, distant embrace.
On the day Oliver secured his admission to college and waving around his acceptance the letter, the Moon was a full moon. On a night forecasted to be dark and cloudy, she was fully visible on a foggy night. Bright and proud yet quiet.
When he was too old to stay at the orphanage, and moved to a university hostel, Oliver kept up his conversations. He didn't know why he did it, only that it brought him comfort. That he enjoyed sitting by the window, soaking in the moonlight. In his mind, he was talking to an invisible parent, far away in the night skies. Watching over him from wherever wonderful people go when they die too early for their time.
A part of him liked to imagine the Moon could hear him.
The rest of him couldn't have known she was always listening, and always proud.

Prompt: [WP] There is a dungeon deemed "coughing baby easy", used by everyone to train rookies, test spells, and as a hangout spot for ordinary children. A roaming frenzied super monster from the MOST dangerous region just took one look at it, froze, became scarily aware of where it was, then fled.
comment:
The townsfolk watched as the Golden Arch-Dragon scrambled in place, desperately trying to gain traction, before speeding off into the nearby forest. They turned back, staring in newfound wonder at their local hangout.
When they first discovered Sproutling’s Cavern, it was seen as little more than a potential training ground—a deep cavern jutting into the side of a large mountain filled with moss-covered ruins of a civilization long past. The small, insect-like monsters that inhabited the cavern made for easy practice for young adventures looking to practice their footwork without being in real danger.
But as time went on, and word of this delightfully harmless “dungeon” spread, it attracted a different kind of monster – tourists. These traveling townsfolks would come in waves to see the cavern that The Adventures Guide to Caves, Dungeons, and Swamps rated half a sword for difficulty but five swords for hospitality. Unlike most caves in the region, the atmosphere in this dungeon was mild, almost humid, a far cry from the icy temperatures of the neighbouring haunts. A warm breeze often flowed through the cavern, providing the feeling like you were standing on the edge of a warm body of water on a sunny day.  Other than jagged stalactites and stalagmites that jutted from the floor and ceiling of the cave, Sproutling’s Cavern acted as the perfect location to raise a family or, even better, franchise a chain restaurant.
After many years, the cavern became a well-known tourist destination across the land, complete with restaurants, bars, and lodgings, all situated within the cave itself.
So, it was with perplexed stares that the townsfolk watched the dragon retreat with its tail between its legs at the sight of their home.
An exploratory committee was assembled to try and ascertain more about Sproutling’s Cavern. Shutting down the Cavern was, of course, out of the question – Feastday was approaching after all, one of the Cavern’s most profitable holiday months, so the committee toiled in the background.
In reality, no one had ventured TOO deep into the cavern before – light was scarce, and the opening of the cave was more than enough to host a thriving economy. The committee’s expedition was halted when they reached the cavern's end – a massive drop, sinking deep into a black abyss. Above the drop, a peculiar rock formation hung…or dangled, as one committee member wrote in their findings. The rock dripped residue down into the massive pit below, and the committee returned to the entrance with no more answers than when they left.
In the decades since the incident, many outside observers have scoffed at the opaqueness of the residents of Sproutling’s Cavern. Time has an interesting way of making the most subtle of red flags ring alarm bells for those who have the benefit of reflecting on disasters.
Did Sproutling’s Cavern’s residents simply ignore the smell wafting from the cave, or did they celebrate it as a unique feature of their home? When the entire mountain around them began to shift, did they assume it was an earthquake? And how could they ignore the grumbling noise coming from deep below, like an appetite slowly beginning to awake from a deep slumber…

Prompt: [WP] An elf realizes their long lifespans makes them the perfect lenders. They decided to protect their forest by engaging in banking services with "long term loans" for the average human, but extremely short for an elf.
comment:
I was a ranger for our village, helping our elder deal with humans.
I was confused why their merchants haggle so much, and fight with their lives for the smallest of benefits.
We elves consider it beneath us, so we always gave in to their demands, supplying them a bit more for a longer period, for less.
It was still profitable to us...or so we thought.
The elder, and one of the merchants finally explained it to me, and I was shook.
I took a vacation for a while, thinking about it...until I managed to think of a way to use it for our village's benefit.
I came up with the idea to lend money, and resources to humans, with a long term, so that they don't have to worry about it for a long time.
For us elves, who live for thousands of years, 5 decades is nothing, for humans is a lifetime.
It was approved by the Elders, and I was made leader of the project.
To protect the village, I forgot my honor, and my pride, and started to deal with the humans.
It was a great success.
Low interest rates, a lot of gold, a long long term loan, and they took the bait willingly.
Merchants, noble houses, even Empires' royal family loaned from our village.
Sometimes, I didn't even want the resources back, but asked for an alliance during the loan period, in which they would come to our aid.
Sometimes, they didn't want to pay it back, and I just had to threaten that we will stop loaning to everyone, and the problems solved themselves.
In a mere 400 years, our forest grew, our village became a town...and we lived happily.
But I...was swamped!
Never would have I imagined how much work it is!
Sure, I hired many of my fellow brothers and sisters, but God...
The humans always wanted to meet me.
As if I was some sort of legend, or rumor only to them, and it's only getting worse.
I never considered that descendants of people I loaned to will come to consider me some sort of...benefactor.
It's good that they feel close to me, to the village...
But it brings unnecessary complications...yet, I can't stop.
More and more elves choose to move to our forest, to our town...and I can't let them down.

Prompt: [WP] You run the foster home in Hell that takes in the firstborn that many who make deals with the Devil sign away. They're inherently innocent, so you treat the children with kindness. One day, you notice your horns have started to shrink and your wings growing feathers.
comment:
I watch as the kids run around, and play in the courtyard.
"Stop using flame magic, Alan! And you, Belle, I get it that you want to become a succubi, but wait at least until you are 18!", I shouted at them.
They were all humans...living in Hell, slowly turning into demons.
And I...I was their caretaker, running this foster home.
After all...they are the firstborn that were given to devils in exchange of the fulfillment of their wishes.
Yeah, it's fucked up, but the devils don't give two flying fucks about these kids.
The moment the kids arrive in Hell, the devils get their rewards from Hell itself...and the kids are left to fend for themselves.
For aeons I watched them be used as toys, slaves, and food, until I decided to make this foster home.
I may be a demon...but even I couldn't take seeing their suffering anymore.
So I created Lezel's Foster home, and it's not a random whim of mine.
As a Space Demon, I can control...you guessed it space.
My foster home looks like a basic house on the outside, but inside...
Let's just put it this way, currently, there are 492.391 kids in my care, and millions have graduated, and joined demon tribes, and clans.
I am proud of my work...but recently, something off was happening.
The kids were laughing, saying that my beautiful, purple horns were...shrinking.
And they were plucking...plucking feathers out of my wings.
It was...ominous.
I tried to shrug it off, but I started to feel more and more...uneasy.
Then a visitor came to my little establishment...someone who used to live here.
"Angelica!", I said to the young woman who came to visit us.
She was a firstborn given to Hell, roughly 10 thousand years ago, who became a witch.
She smiled at me, then looked me up and down...and sighed.
"Well uncle Lezel...it's just as I feared.", she said.
I frowned, knowing that she specialized in diseases and ailments.
"Am I dying?", I asked.
She looked around, chasing the eavesdropping kids away, before shaking her head.
"Worse...you are ascending.
Demon Lezel...you are about to become an angel.", she said.
I froze.
I looked around...looked at the kids...at the life I built...and shivered.
I can't lose this...

Prompt: [WP] The aliens you've seen while living out in the woods have rarely been "friendly," but always benign. You have your space, they have theirs, rarely interacting... which is why you knew something was wrong when you found advanced defenses around your house and a hand-drawn warning to stay inside.
comment:
Well now this is different.
The last time they had tried to communicate they had done little more than crudely scratch barely-identifiable pictograms into the trees surrounding my cabin. Something that might generously have been a rabbit, or a deer, perhaps? With no discernable meaning attached. That was fine, I could disregard that.
But this?
I turn the note over in my hand again. I have so many questions.
Where did they get paper? This isn't anything like the notebooks I have in the cabin - they haven't stolen it from me.
What have they written in? It certainly doesn't look like any sort of ink I'm used to. What is the blue-ish green sheen to it?
But most worrying of all, how have they learnt English?! They've never so much as uttered a sound when I've seen them out in the woods, even their appearance and fleeting skitters are eerily silent. Maybe they've only learnt to read and write. Maybe they still wouldn't be able to talk back to me... But that doesn't make this any less upsetting.
Indeed, the hairs on the back of my neck haven't sat flat since I found this note slid awkwardly underneath my door.
AND THAT'S ANOTHER THING!
They've never been within sight of this place before! I thought we had an understanding - if I see them, I stay away from whatever they're doing, and they in turn leave me the hell alone. This is tantamount to a declaration of war!
Except... what would I fight them with? They don't exactly seem scared of my dad's old rifle. When I shoot it I get shaken up by the noise, but I've never seen them so much as flinch. I've pretty much convinced myself that it wouldn't even touch them.
What'll I do, swing fire at them?
Maybe I should just burn this whole damn forest down. Mum'd be happy with that, wherever the hell she is now. Would serve everyone right.
'Stay inside'
Scratched out in awkward yet unmistakeable letters.
I almost want to believe this is the work of some local prankster. Somebody playing on my famed 'paranoia', but that just can't be true. I'm too far out, and besides, it's not like anyone's ever missed me.
No, it has to be them.
I pull the tiniest corner of my curtain aside, and peer out into the trees. It's still some hours until sunrise, so my eyes take a moment to adjust to the darkness. As they do, I grow sick to my stomach.
Off beyond the trees are dozens - no, hundreds - of pairs of eyes, staring back at me. Unblinking, and, as far as I can tell, unfeeling.
Watching.
Waiting.
I sink down and let the curtain fall back across the window. I struggle to lift my leaden arms, and eventually give up.
Welp, guess I'm staying in here for a while.

Prompt: [WP] "So, what immortality do you have?" "What?" "Well everybody in this room has a type of immortality, I got hyper regeneration, the guy over the is a lich, the girl in leather can save and reload, and I am not bothered enough to keep talking so what is your immortality?" "Memory"
comment:
I entered the room, where a dozen or so entities were already waiting.
From floating skulls, to Titans the size of mountains, I saw a variety of interesting individuals.
"Greetings, welcome to the gathering.
So, what immortality do you have?", a gentleman approached me.
This indeed was a gathering I finally chose to attend...a gathering of immortals.
"Hello...What do you mean?", I asked.
The gentleman smiled, and gestured to the other attendees.
"Let's start, well...that guy there is a lich, that girl over there munching on cupcakes has save points.
I have hyper regeneration, the Titan has invulnerability to everything, time included....
And a few more, so what's yours?", he asked.
"Memory.", I said, walking towards the table.
"Memory? What does that mean?", the girl munching on cupcakes asked.
"It means as long as my memory lives, so do I.", I said.
This attracted the attention of most of them...
Yeah, it was a bit cocky.
"You say it as if you were truly immortal...
But wouldn't that mean if the planet or planets your memory lives on are destroyed, you die as well?", the Titan asked, snorting.
"That's why I became a interdimensional writer.", I chuckled.
This confused them even more...all, but the lich.
"Hoh...you write books with yourself as the character or characters...and spread them through the universe, thus they remember you...
It's still gambling, isn't it?", it asked.
I laughed.
"Not just this universe, but all of them, and in different times, and to me it's not gambling...
For I am a decent writer.", I said.
They all quieted down, and surrounded me.
I chuckled awkwardly, feeling I might have been too...forward? Too cocky?
I am not good at socializing.
"Ahm, sorry if I...", I started.
Before I could finish my apology, they all laughed, and patted my shoulders.
"Good! Then we truly welcome you here!
God, we aren't many, immortals that is, and even less are enjoying socializing...
So we are happy to hear you are confident in your immortality, and we hope you will join our centennial meetings!", the gentleman who welcomed me said.
I nodded.
They smiled, and we started discussing about everything and anything, laughing, joking, exchanging ideas...
It was so good, I wondered why I haven't joined it earlier...
